Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

shot noun

from a gun, or an arrow

also gunshot, shots, fire a shot, shoot (a gun), shoot (an arrow), a shot rang out

modern

M-O s.v. gunshot (Tursellinus 1652: ictū sclopī)

ictus sclopētī

phrase: ictus, ictūs m. with the genitive of sclopētum

a gunshot

Classical ictus is a blow or stroke, and also the hit of a missile shot from an engine (ictū scorpiōnis, Caes. B.G. 7.25); with sclopētī it is the Renaissance phrase for a gunshot. A cannon shot is ictus tormentī (M-O s.v. gunfire).

Other words

  • sclopētō — to fire a gun, shoot

    verb, first conjugation (sclopētāre) · also used · modern · Traupman 324

    Traupman’s verb. M-O gives sclopētum displōdere, to fire a gun, and plumbeā glande ferīre, to shoot someone (M-O s.v. gunshot).

  • tēla conjicere — to shoot (arrows, spears, missiles)

    phrase: tēlum, tēlī n. with conjiciō, conjicere, conjēcī, conjectum · also used · classical · Caes. B.G. 1.26: tēla in nostrōs (Lewis & Short)

    The classical way to say shooting, of bows, slings and spears: sagittās conjicere, to shoot arrows.

Examples

  • nōn caecīs ictibus procul ex imprōvīsō vulnerābantur

    they were not wounded by blind shots from afar, without warningLiv. 34.14.11 (Lewis & Short)

See also gun, target, weapon, hit the target.

SourcesLewis & Short: ictus · Lewis & Short: conicio
